A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main text, equations, Tables 1–2, Figures 1–7, and Appendix A are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original ImageNet-1K attack experiments, comparisons against baseline attacks, VLLM evaluations, and computational-redundancy experiments in Appendix A.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results, including Tables 1–2, the VLLM comparison in Figure 6, and the appendix experiments in Figure 7.

M1.justification: The attention sparsity and permutation operations, clean-token regularization, ghost MoE, robust-token strategies, and online policy remain unchanged. The PiT and Swin adaptations are also retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same ImageNet-1K tasks, CNN/ViT targets, four VLLMs, and appendix perturbation scenarios. The newly cited StatLLM dataset is not used in an experiment.

E2.justification: Table 2 and Figure 6 retain the same MI-, NI-, EMI-, VMI-FGSM, PGN, DTA, TGR, GNS, and FPR comparisons. The exclusion of TGR, GNS, and FPR for Swin-T is unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported settings remain unchanged, including 1,000 ImageNet images, perturbation budget 16/255, 10 attack steps, momentum decay 1, and VLLM prompting with 1,000 candidate labels.

E4.justification: Figures 2–5 retain the same operation and parameter studies. Table 1 retains the dynamic/global robust-token comparison, and Appendix A retains the token, attention-weight, attention-head, and FFN-neuron dropping analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Both retain the same point estimates and cross-model averages.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–2 and plotted results in Figures 2–7 are unchanged. Table 2 still reports proposed-method averages of 86.9%, 87.4%, and 88.9% for ViT-B/16, PiT-B, and Swin-T surrogates, respectively.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, equations (1)–(10), and policy-gradient derivation are unchanged. No formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs are added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about exploiting computational redundancy, the proposed operations and online strategy, and attack effectiveness across architectures.

C2.justification: Interpretations of sparsity, shared attention information, clean-token regularization, expert diversity, and efficiency-versus-transferability tradeoffs are unchanged. Appendix A retains its redundancy explanations, with no new limitations.

D1.justification: Implementation descriptions, hyperparameters, and token-placement instructions are unchanged. The added author email provides general contact information rather than new technical details or code/data access instructions.

R1.justification: v3 adds Min et al. (2024), Applied statistics in the era of artificial intelligence, and two Song et al. (2025) works on StatLLM and statistical programming. These are cited in Sections 1–2 without expanding the existing attack-method or redundancy positioning.

P1.justification: v3 adds an author contact email, removes 'Under review' from the first-page footer, and changes 'appendix A' to 'section A'. The narrative, section order, and substantive explanations remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The added citations cause limited text and bibliography reflow, particularly on pages 12–14, alongside small front-page and typesetting changes. All figures and tables retain their designs, captions, and placement.

improvement.justification: The scientific arguments, experimental evidence in Tables 1–2 and Figures 2–7, and Appendix A are unchanged. The three added references receive no substantive explanation connecting them to the work, while contact and formatting edits offer only administrative refinements. These localized changes leave overall quality essentially unchanged.
